title: First the row, then the audience
hookLine: anyone who comes to see the Guru eats first in langar; tradition says the emperor Akbar sat on the floor too

cards: Meeting someone important usually works the same way. A waiting room, a line, a list, and someone at a desk deciding who goes first. The more important the visitor, the shorter the wait.

At Goindval, visiting Guru Amar Das worked differently. Before anyone at all could sit with the Guru, they first had to sit on the floor in the langar, the community kitchen, in a row with everyone else, and eat.
Farmers, merchants, beggars, priests. And one day, tradition says, the Mughal emperor himself came to Goindval: Akbar.

teach.b: Sikhs sum up the rule in a short Punjabi saying: pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat. First the row, then the gathering.

teach.h: PANGAT — THE ROW ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: The pangat is the row of people sitting side by side on the floor to eat; the sangat is the gathering around the Guru. The order matters. You don't get to the Guru until you've eaten as an equal with everyone else.
Tradition says Akbar honored the rule.

teach.h: THE EMPEROR SAT IN THE ROW.
teach.b: The emperor sat down on the floor in the row, among ordinary people, and ate the simple food of the kitchen before he met Guru Amar Das.
Some tellings add that he was so moved he offered the Guru a grant of land, and the Guru declined it, saying the kitchen should be supported by the community's own work and giving, not by a king.
Historians note that the visit comes to us through Sikh tradition, and the details vary. But the rule itself is still kept today. Yesterday it was water; today it's food.
A shared meal says who counts as your equal, and in that world rules of rank and caste said who could sit and eat with whom. The pangat wipes that line out, on the floor, every day.
Nobody sits at the head. Nobody gets a higher seat.
The same food, from the same pot, served by volunteers. Guru Nanak had begun the langar, and Mata Khivi had kept it going. Guru Amar Das made it the doorway.
Before you meet the Guru, you meet your neighbor, at eye level, on the floor.

how: In gurdwaras, langar is served to anyone who comes, seated together in rows on the floor, in pangat; the saying pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat is often quoted to explain why.

games.q: you're the emperor of India, arriving at Goindval to meet the Guru. you're told everyone eats in the row on the floor first. what do you do?
o: sit on the floor in the row and eat.
send a servant to eat for you.
games.why: tradition says Akbar sat in the pangat and ate with everyone else before he met Guru Amar Das.

practice: Picture the row: faces side by side, all at the same height. At your next meal, sit where you usually don't, and let someone else be served first, or serve everyone yourself and sit down last.
If you eat alone, eat on the floor or at a counter, somewhere without a head of the table.

wordCard.voice: Pangat. The row where everyone, even an emperor, sat on the floor at Goindval and ate as equals before meeting the Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, a row; the line of people seated side by side for langar.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody sits at the head. Tomorrow, the preachers, women and men. Until tomorrow.
